_comment: Developers series, film 6: slides and a run in FreeXmlToolkit (FundsXmlDevRegulatoryDocVideo), on the realistic example Multi-Asset-Derivatives-Fund_2025-10.xml.

description.en: How the FinDatEx templates sit in a FundsXML file: RegulatoryReportings with DirectReporting and IndirectReporting, an EMT V4.2 block (data set information, general information, target market, ex-ante costs) and a TPT V7 block for Solvency II (portfolio data, positions with CIC codes and valuations), template versions as their own elements, and how country-specific data and custom attributes extend the standard.

say.en: In this film you look inside the regulatory part of a FundsXML file: an EMT block for distributors, and a TPT block for insurers. It takes about five minutes.

items.head: DirectReporting
items.text: EMT, EET, EFT, KIIDs, PRIIPs KIDs, EMIR.

items.head: IndirectReporting
items.text: TPT for Solvency II, PRIIPs data (EPT).

say.en: All regulatory data sits in one block at the top level: RegulatoryReportings. It splits into two branches. Direct reporting holds templates that describe the fund or share class itself, such as EMT and EET. Indirect reporting holds data that others use for their own reporting, such as the TPT for insurers and PRIIPs data. Each template version is an element of its own.

Here it is in the file, after the asset master data. Regulatory reportings, then direct reporting, and inside it the element EMT V four two: the European MiFID Template in version four point two. This example file is written for FundsXML four point two point nine; newer schema versions add EMT four point three as an element of its own.

An EMT block describes one financial instrument, here the euro retail class; the file has one for each share class. Data set information names the template version, the producer and which parts are reported. General information identifies the share class by its ISIN, and gives its name, its currency, and whether it distributes.

The target market follows the MiFID categories: which investor types the fund is meant for, their knowledge and experience, their ability to bear losses, the risk indicator, here three, and the client objectives: capital growth, with a recommended holding period of five years.

And the ex-ante costs: ongoing costs, management fee, transaction costs and incidental costs, given as decimal fractions of the net asset value. Zero point zero one five eight means one point five eight percent.

Below, in indirect reporting, the Tripartite Template in version seven. At portfolio level: the TPT version, the identifier of the share class, its name and currency, the fund's total net assets, the valuation date and the reporting date.

Then the positions. Each one starts with its CIC code, the Complementary Identification Code: four characters for the country of quotation and the kind of instrument. U S three one is a listed equity quoted in the United States, here the same fictional share we met in the portfolio. Then the instrument code and name, and the valuation: quantity, market values in quotation and portfolio currency, and the weight. Credit risk data names the issuer, its country and its economic sector.

Further down is a government bond. Its CIC code is D E one one: a government bond quoted in Germany. For bonds, the template adds the interest rate data: rate type, coupon rate and frequency, and the redemption with its maturity date. Together with the modified duration below, that is the information an insurer needs for its interest rate and spread risk.

en.title: The other templates, the same way

items.head: Older versions
items.text: Remain available for a transition period.

say.en: The other templates work the same way. The EET for sustainability data and the EFT for feedback from distributors sit in direct reporting. The PRIIPs data of the EPT sits in indirect reporting. Each has its own element per version, and older versions remain in the schema for a transition period, so sender and receiver can move to a new version when both are ready.

items.head: Flags
items.text: Y and N, sometimes more letters.

items.head: Check each field
items.text: The template's documentation, not the core's habits.

say.en: Templates follow their own conventions, and they differ from the core of FundsXML. Flags are single letters, Y and N. Percentages are often decimal fractions, where one stands for one hundred percent. And many fields are numbered codes from the template's own lists, for example code one for an ISIN as the identifier type. Read the template's documentation for each field, and do not assume the conventions of the core.

items.head: Core
items.text: Funds, share classes, positions, assets: neutral.

items.head: Converter
items.text: Derives template fields from the core.

items.head: Template block
items.text: The view a regulation asks for: EMT, TPT …

say.en: One thing is worth knowing. Much of what the templates ask for also exists in the core of FundsXML: identifiers, values, issuers and dates. The core describes funds and assets neutrally; a template block is a view of that data in the form a regulation asks for. Converters can fill a template from the core data, so the same fact is not maintained twice.

items.head: CountrySpecificData
items.text: National reporting, for example Austria and Germany.

items.head: Sparingly
items.text: Agree on them in writing; propose common needs for the standard.

say.en: And when you need more? Country-specific data carries national reporting at the top level and in several blocks, for example for Austria and Germany. Custom attributes let partners exchange extra fields in a defined way, without breaking the schema. Use them sparingly, and agree on them in writing.
That was the regulatory part of a FundsXML file. In the next film, you see how documents such as key information documents travel in FundsXML. Thanks for watching.
